claim: Piezo1 ion channels mediate the conversion of mechanical forces into electrical signals.
source: Piezo1 ion channels mediate the conversion of mechanical forces into electrical signals and are critical for responsiveness to touch in metazoans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about Piezo1 function, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Piezo1 ion channels are critical for responsiveness to touch in metazoans.
source: Piezo1 ion channels mediate the conversion of mechanical forces into electrical signals and are critical for responsiveness to touch in metazoans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Piezo1's physiological role.

claim: The apparent mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1 varies substantially across cellular environments, stimulating methods and protocols.
source: The apparent mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1 varies substantially across cellular environments, stimulating methods and protocols, raising the fundamental questions of what precise physical stimulus activates the channel and how its stimulus sensitivity is regulated.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivates the research questions.

claim: Piezo1 responds to lateral membrane tension with exquisite sensitivity as compared to other mechanically activated channels.
source: We find that Piezo1 responds to lateral membrane tension with exquisite sensitivity as compared to other mechanically activated channels and that resting tension can drive channel inactivation, thereby tuning overall mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing T50 values.

claim: Resting tension can drive channel inactivation of Piezo1.
source: We find that Piezo1 responds to lateral membrane tension with exquisite sensitivity as compared to other mechanically activated channels and that resting tension can drive channel inactivation, thereby tuning overall mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by prepulse experiments.

claim: Resting tension tunes overall mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1.
source: We find that Piezo1 responds to lateral membrane tension with exquisite sensitivity as compared to other mechanically activated channels and that resting tension can drive channel inactivation, thereby tuning overall mechanical sensitivity of Piezo1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by prepulse experiments showing changes in T50.

claim: Mechanosensation is essential for cells ranging from bacteria to human fingertips.
source: Mechanosensation is essential for cells ranging from bacteria, which must regulate cell volume in response to harsh osmotic stress, to Merkel cells and sensory neurons in human fingertips, which are exquisitely sensitive to gentle touch (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: Bacteria must regulate cell volume in response to harsh osmotic stress.
source: Mechanosensation is essential for cells ranging from bacteria, which must regulate cell volume in response to harsh osmotic stress, to Merkel cells and sensory neurons in human fingertips, which are exquisitely sensitive to gentle touch (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: Merkel cells and sensory neurons in human fingertips are exquisitely sensitive to gentle touch.
source: Mechanosensation is essential for cells ranging from bacteria, which must regulate cell volume in response to harsh osmotic stress, to Merkel cells and sensory neurons in human fingertips, which are exquisitely sensitive to gentle touch (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: Mechanosensation is initiated through the opening of mechanosensitive ion channels.
source: Mechanosensation is initiated through the opening of mechanosensitive ion channels, including the K2P family in vertebrates, NOMPC in Drosophila, and the DEG/ENaC family in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: The K2P family of mechanosensitive ion channels is found in vertebrates.
source: Mechanosensation is initiated through the opening of mechanosensitive ion channels, including the K2P family in vertebrates, NOMPC in Drosophila, and the DEG/ENaC family in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: NOMPC is a mechanosensitive ion channel in Drosophila.
source: Mechanosensation is initiated through the opening of mechanosensitive ion channels, including the K2P family in vertebrates, NOMPC in Drosophila, and the DEG/ENaC family in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: The DEG/ENaC family of mechanosensitive ion channels is found in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Mechanosensation is initiated through the opening of mechanosensitive ion channels, including the K2P family in vertebrates, NOMPC in Drosophila, and the DEG/ENaC family in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2015.

claim: Piezo proteins were identified as the pore-forming subunits of an excitatory mechanosensitive channel in metazoans.
source: Recently, Piezo proteins were identified as the pore-forming subunits of an excitatory (non-selective cation) mechanosensitive channel in metazoans (Coste et al., 2010; 2012; Faucherre et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2012; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo channels are non-selective cation channels.
source: Recently, Piezo proteins were identified as the pore-forming subunits of an excitatory (non-selective cation) mechanosensitive channel in metazoans (Coste et al., 2010; 2012; Faucherre et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2012; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezos are large proteins with >2500 residues.
source: Piezos are large proteins with >2500 residues that lack homology to any known proteins (Coste et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2015.

claim: Piezos lack homology to any known proteins.
source: Piezos are large proteins with >2500 residues that lack homology to any known proteins (Coste et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2015.

claim: There are two mammalian Piezo isoforms: Piezo1 and Piezo2.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are widely expressed.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 play key roles in vascular development.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 play key roles in red blood cell volume regulation.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 play key roles in lineage choice in neural stem cells.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 play key roles in touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons.
source: The two mammalian isoforms, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are widely expressed and play key roles in many physiological processes, including vascular development, red blood cell volume regulation, lineage choice in neural stem cells, and touch sensation in Merkel cells and DRG neurons (Cahalan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Knockout of either Piezo1 or Piezo2 is lethal in mouse.
source: In mouse, knockout of either isoform is lethal, further emphasizing the functional importance of the protein (Ranade et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ranade et al., 2014a.

claim: The activation mechanism of Piezos, including the precise physical stimulus that initiates pore opening, is unknown.
source: Despite an increased understanding of the various roles Piezos play in many biological processes, the activation mechanism, including the precise physical stimulus that initiates pore opening (gating), is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the research.

claim: The recent medium-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of mouse Piezo1 revealed many features of the coarse channel architecture.
source: The recent medium-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of mouse Piezo1 revealed many features of the coarse channel architecture, but does not provide conclusive clues about the activation mechanism (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ge et al., 2015.

claim: The cryo-electron microscopy structure of mouse Piezo1 does not provide conclusive clues about the activation mechanism.
source: The recent medium-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of mouse Piezo1 revealed many features of the coarse channel architecture, but does not provide conclusive clues about the activation mechanism (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ge et al., 2015.

claim: In vivo, Piezos respond to diverse forces, including laminar flow and cellular compression.
source: In vivo, Piezos respond to diverse forces, including laminar flow and cellular compression (Lee et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two techniques used to evoke Piezo channel activity in heterologous systems are direct stimulation with a blunt glass pipette and application of negative pressure to stretch the membrane in a patch pipette.
source: In heterologous systems, two techniques used to evoke channel activity are direct stimulation of the cell by touching with a blunt glass pipette and application of negative pressure to stretch the membrane in a patch pipette (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: Lateral membrane tension is the stimulus for the bacterial mechanosensitive ion channel MscL.
source: For example, lateral membrane tension is the stimulus for the well-characterized bacterial mechanosensitive ion channel MscL (Moe and Blount, 2005; Sukharev et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moe and Blount, 2005 and Sukharev et al., 1999.

claim: No accessory proteins of Piezos have been identified that could tether the channel to the cellular matrix.
source: To date, no accessory proteins of Piezos have been identified that could tether the channel to the cellular matrix, suggesting that, as for MscL, the activating stimulus may be directly transmitted through the bilayer.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: The activating stimulus for Piezos may be directly transmitted through the bilayer.
source: To date, no accessory proteins of Piezos have been identified that could tether the channel to the cellular matrix, suggesting that, as for MscL, the activating stimulus may be directly transmitted through the bilayer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of identified accessory proteins and comparison to MscL.

claim: During a sustained stimulus, Piezo currents decay (inactivate) with a typical time course of tens of milliseconds.
source: A key feature of Piezos is that during a sustained stimulus, currents decay (inactivate) with a typical time course of tens of milliseconds, suggesting continuous modulation of channel availability (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: Piezo mutations that alter inactivation kinetics are linked to several human diseases.
source: Consistent with a high physiological importance for inactivation, Piezo mutations that alter inactivation kinetics are linked to several human diseases, including dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis, xerocytosis, Marden-Walker and Gordon syndromes, and distal arthrogryposis (Albuisson et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013; Coste et al., 2013; McMillin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several Piezo gain-of-function mutations reduce the rate and/or extent of inactivation and apparently sensitize Piezos to pressure.
source: Importantly, several of these gain-of-function mutations not only reduce the rate and/or extent of inactivation, but also apparently sensitize Piezos to pressure (Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bae et al., 2013.

claim: Yoda1 is the only known agonist for Piezo ion channels.
source: Additionally, the only known agonist for Piezo ion channels, Yoda1, both sensitizes Piezo1 to pressure and slows inactivation (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Syeda et al., 2015.

claim: Yoda1 sensitizes Piezo1 to pressure and slows inactivation.
source: Additionally, the only known agonist for Piezo ion channels, Yoda1, both sensitizes Piezo1 to pressure and slows inactivation (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Syeda et al., 2015.

claim: The pressure sensitivity of Piezos varies with cell type, with half-maximal pressure for activation for Piezo1 ranging from ~−15 to −40 mmHg.
source: The pressure sensitivity of Piezos also varies with cell type, with previous reports of half-maximal pressure for activation for Piezo1 ranging from ~−15 to −40 mmHg (Coste et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo sensitivity is modulated by proteins including EPAC1 and STOML3.
source: Piezo sensitivity is also modulated by proteins including EPAC1 and STOML3; differential expression of these and other modulators both among cells and within a single cell may also regulate the overall sensitivity (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013; Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eijkelkamp et al., 2013 and Poole et al., 2014.

claim: Piezo1 is activated by membrane tension with a high degree of sensitivity (T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m).
source: We find that Piezo1 is activated by membrane tension with a high degree of sensitivity (T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m) and that this sensitivity is directly influenced by resting membrane tension.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Piezo1 sensitivity to membrane tension is directly influenced by resting membrane tension.
source: We find that Piezo1 is activated by membrane tension with a high degree of sensitivity (T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m) and that this sensitivity is directly influenced by resting membrane tension.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: In cell-attached patches, negative pressure induced rapidly-inactivating inward currents at −80 mV that are characteristic of Piezo1 ion channels.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed that in cell-attached patches, negative pressure induced rapidly-inactivating inward currents at −80 mV that are characteristic of Piezo1 ion channels (Coste et al., 2010; 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and citations to previous reports.

claim: Piezo1 currents first became apparent at −5 mmHg in cell-attached patches.
source: Currents first became apparent at −5 mmHg, increased with the magnitude of pressure, and reached saturation at ~−30 mmHg (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Piezo1 currents increased with the magnitude of negative pressure in cell-attached patches.
source: Currents first became apparent at −5 mmHg, increased with the magnitude of pressure, and reached saturation at ~−30 mmHg (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Piezo1 currents reached saturation at ~−30 mmHg in cell-attached patches.
source: Currents first became apparent at −5 mmHg, increased with the magnitude of pressure, and reached saturation at ~−30 mmHg (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Negative pressure induced a convex curvature of the membrane in cell-attached patches.
source: As expected, our simultaneous imaging approach revealed that negative pressure also induced a convex curvature of the membrane and that the radius of curvature decreased with increasing magnitudes of pressure (Figure 1A; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The radius of curvature decreased with increasing magnitudes of negative pressure in cell-attached patches.
source: As expected, our simultaneous imaging approach revealed that negative pressure also induced a convex curvature of the membrane and that the radius of curvature decreased with increasing magnitudes of pressure (Figure 1A; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Positive pressure inverted the membrane curvature to concave in cell-attached patches.
source: We therefore applied positive pressure to our membrane patches, which indeed inverted the membrane curvature.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Piezo1 currents were reliably induced by positive pressure in cell-attached patches.
source: Piezo1 currents were also reliably induced by this positive pressure protocol (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pressure responses to positive pressure were right-shifted compared to negative pressure in cell-attached patches.
source: Peak current amplitudes again increased with the magnitude of pressure, albeit with a striking difference: pressure responses were right-shifted, as currents first became apparent at +15 mmHg and often did not reach saturation before rupture of the patch.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Piezo1 currents to positive pressure first became apparent at +15 mmHg in cell-attached patches.
source: Peak current amplitudes again increased with the magnitude of pressure, albeit with a striking difference: pressure responses were right-shifted, as currents first became apparent at +15 mmHg and often did not reach saturation before rupture of the patch.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Small currents were observed upon release of small (+5 mmHg) positive pressure stimuli in cell-attached patches.
source: Interestingly, we also often observed small currents upon release of small (+5 mmHg) positive pressure stimuli, discussed further below.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In cellular membranes, Piezo1 is activated by both convex and concave membrane curvature.
source: Together, these observations suggest that in cellular membranes, Piezo1 is activated by both convex and concave membrane curvature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing activation by both positive and negative pressure.

claim: Both positive and negative pressure evoked transient inward currents through Piezo1 ion channels in inside-out patches.
source: For inside-out patches, both positive and negative pressure again evoked transient inward currents through Piezo1 ion channels (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The optical density of the membrane was reduced in inside-out patches compared to cell-attached patches.
source: In this patch configuration, the optical density of the membrane was reduced compared to cell-attached patches, consistent with the idea that less cytoskeleton is retained in a cell-detached configuration (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by imaging observations and a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009.

claim: Less cytoskeleton is retained in inside-out patches compared to cell-attached patches.
source: In this patch configuration, the optical density of the membrane was reduced compared to cell-attached patches, consistent with the idea that less cytoskeleton is retained in a cell-detached configuration (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009 and inference from optical density observations.

claim: Both positive and negative pressure robustly activated Piezo1 currents in outside-out patches.
source: Still, we obtained the same result as for the other patch configurations: both positive and negative pressure robustly activated Piezo1 currents (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Decay of currents was not consistently observed in the outside-out configuration.
source: In contrast to cell-attached and inside-out patches, we did not consistently observe decay of currents elicited in the outside-out configuration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Only negligible currents were elicited in cells transfected with empty vector (pcDNA).
source: In all of the above experiments, only negligible currents were elicited in cells transfected with empty vector (pcDNA), showing that the currents induced by membrane curvature are specifically mediated by Piezo1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The currents induced by membrane curvature are specifically mediated by Piezo1.
source: In all of the above experiments, only negligible currents were elicited in cells transfected with empty vector (pcDNA), showing that the currents induced by membrane curvature are specifically mediated by Piezo1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiments with empty vector.

claim: Currents elicited by positive pressure in outside-out patches were typically larger than in other configurations.
source: Specifically, currents elicited by positive pressure in outside-out patches were typically larger than in the other configurations, consistent with the observation that a larger surface area of membrane is preserved within the confines of the gigaseal in this configuration (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A larger surface area of membrane is preserved within the confines of the gigaseal in outside-out patches.
source: Specifically, currents elicited by positive pressure in outside-out patches were typically larger than in the other configurations, consistent with the observation that a larger surface area of membrane is preserved within the confines of the gigaseal in this configuration (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Currents elicited by positive pressure in inside-out patches were small.
source: In contrast, currents elicited by positive pressure in inside-out patches were small, likely because patches that survived multiple positive pressure pulses were biased towards those made using smaller pipettes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cell-attached patches stimulated with negative pressure required less pressure for activation (P50 = −16.7 ± 2.8 mmHg) than inside-out patches (P50 = −35.8 ± 4.0 mmHg).
source: Cell-attached patches stimulated with negative pressure required less pressure for activation (P5o = −16.7 ± 2.8 mmHg; N=15) than inside-out patches (P50 = −35.8 ± 4.0 mmHg; N=10; P<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Cell-attached and inside-out patches required similar pressures for activation with positive pressure.
source: In contrast, cell-attached and inside-out patches required similar pressures for activation with positive pressure (cell-attached: P50 = +19.3 ± 1.2 mmHg; N=12; inside-out: P50 = +26.7 ± 4.2 mmHg; N=7; P>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Outside-out patches required much larger pressures for activation than other configurations.
source: For outside-out patches, much larger pressures were required for activation than other configurations (positive pressure: P50 = +70.0 ± 9.6 mmHg; N=11; negative pressure: P50 = −39.8 ± 3.1 mmHg; N = 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Piezo1 can be activated by both convex and concave membrane curvature.
source: Together, these experiments provide strong evidence that Piezo1 can be activated by both convex and concave membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from multiple patch configurations.

claim: Piezo1 sensitivity to a given stimulus may vary significantly with the amount of cytoskeletal content and its sidedness.
source: Further, as cytoskeletal content varies with patch configuration, the different sensitivities we observed among configurations and with convex versus concave geometry suggests that Piezo1 sensitivity to a given stimulus (in this case, pressure) may vary significantly with the amount of cytoskeletal content and its sidedness, i.e., whether the cytoskeleton is subjected into a convex vs. concave geometry (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and supported by a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009.

claim: The radius of curvature (R) of a surface exposed to a pressure difference (Δp) is directly related to lateral tension (T), as described by Laplace's law: T = R·Δp/2.
source: The radius of curvature (R) of a surface exposed to a pressure difference (Δp) is directly related to lateral tension (T), as described by Laplace's law: T = R·Δp/2.
evidence: This is established physical knowledge (Laplace's law).

claim: Curvature can be either positive or negative (convex or concave), but tension is a symmetrical quantity.
source: However, while curvature can be either positive or negative (convex or concave), tension is a symmetrical quantity.
evidence: This is established physical knowledge about the properties of curvature and tension.

claim: The fact that Piezo1 ion channels respond well to both convex and concave curvature suggests qualitatively that Piezo1 might be activated by lateral membrane tension.
source: The fact that Piezo1 ion channels respond well to both convex and concave curvature therefore suggests qualitatively that Piezo1 might be activated by lateral membrane tension.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and the physical properties of tension.

claim: For cell-attached patches, Piezo1 channel activity is well described by a Boltzmann function with a tension of half-maximal activation T50 = 2.7 ± 0.1 mN/m and a slope factor k = 0.8 ± 0.1.
source: For cell-attached patches, we found that Piezo1 channel activity is well described by a Boltzmann function with a tension of half-maximal activation T50 = 2.7 ± 0.1 mN/m and a slope factor k = 0.8 ± 0.1 (N = 15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For inside-out patches, Piezo1 channel activity is well described by a Boltzmann function with T50 = 4.7 ± 0.3 mN/m and k = 1.2 ± 0.1.
source: Similarly, for inside-out patches, the distribution was also well-described by a Boltzmann function; however, patches required slightly more tension for activation (T50 = 4.7 ± 0.3 mN/m; N = 10; P<0.001 vs cell-attached) and had a shallower slope factor (k = 1.2 ± 0.1; P<0.001 vs. cell-attached).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inside-out patches required slightly more tension for activation than cell-attached patches.
source: Similarly, for inside-out patches, the distribution was also well-described by a Boltzmann function; however, patches required slightly more tension for activation (T50 = 4.7 ± 0.3 mN/m; N = 10; P<0.001 vs cell-attached) and had a shallower slope factor (k = 1.2 ± 0.1; P<0.001 vs. cell-attached).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The likelihood of a given pulse leading to patch rupture increased sharply starting around 10 mN/m in both cell-attached and inside-out configurations.
source: Notably, in both configurations the likelihood of a given pulse leading to patch rupture increased sharply starting around 10 mN/m; this is consistent with the lytic tension of the gigaseal, previously reported to be ~10 mN/m (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009.

claim: The lytic tension of the gigaseal is ~10 mN/m.
source: Notably, in both configurations the likelihood of a given pulse leading to patch rupture increased sharply starting around 10 mN/m; this is consistent with the lytic tension of the gigaseal, previously reported to be ~10 mN/m (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009.

claim: Piezo1 activation is consistent with membrane tension as the principal stimulus.
source: Together, these results demonstrate quantitatively that Piezo1 activation is consistent with membrane tension as the principal stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Boltzmann relationships between tension and activation.

claim: Piezo1 is a tension sensor with higher sensitivity than previously reported for other mechanically activated ion channels such as MscS and MscL.
source: In addition, this reveals that Piezo1 is a tension sensor with higher sensitivity than previously reported for other mechanically activated ion channels such as MscS and MscL, (T50 = ~5 mN/m and ~10 mN/m, respectively, when reconstituted in asolectin liposomes or lipid bilayers (Moe and Blount, 2005; Nomura et al., 2012; Sukharev, 2002; Sukharev et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the measured T50 for Piezo1 with published values for MscS and MscL.

claim: MscS has a T50 of ~5 mN/m when reconstituted in asolectin liposomes or lipid bilayers.
source: In addition, this reveals that Piezo1 is a tension sensor with higher sensitivity than previously reported for other mechanically activated ion channels such as MscS and MscL, (T50 = ~5 mN/m and ~10 mN/m, respectively, when reconstituted in asolectin liposomes or lipid bilayers (Moe and Blount, 2005; Nomura et al., 2012; Sukharev, 2002; Sukharev et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MscL has a T50 of ~10 mN/m when reconstituted in asolectin liposomes or lipid bilayers.
source: In addition, this reveals that Piezo1 is a tension sensor with higher sensitivity than previously reported for other mechanically activated ion channels such as MscS and MscL, (T50 = ~5 mN/m and ~10 mN/m, respectively, when reconstituted in asolectin liposomes or lipid bilayers (Moe and Blount, 2005; Nomura et al., 2012; Sukharev, 2002; Sukharev et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The resting tension in a cell-attached gigaseal patch has been estimated to be on the order of 0.5–4.0 mN/m.
source: The resting tension in a cell-attached gigaseal patch has previously been estimated to be on the order of 0.5–4.0 mN/m, which is similar in magnitude to the tension of half-maximal activation (T50 = 2.7 ± 0.1 mN/m) we determined in cell-attached patches (Opsahl and Webb, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Opsahl and Webb, 1994.

claim: Membrane patches are already substantially curved at rest (Δp = 0 mmHg).
source: Additionally, we observed that membrane patches are already substantially curved at rest, i.e. in the absence of any external pressure difference (Δp = 0 mmHg) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Even at rest (Δp = 0 mmHg), a substantial fraction of Piezo1 ion channels might be stimulated and subsequently inactivated.
source: We therefore hypothesized that even at rest (Δp = 0 mmHg), a substantial fraction of Piezo1 ion channels might be stimulated and subsequently inactivated.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observations of resting curvature and tension.

claim: A small positive pressure stimulus that precisely compensates the resting curvature should effectively zero membrane tension in the patch dome.
source: From this, we predicted that a small positive pressure stimulus, that precisely compensates the resting curvature, should effectively zero membrane tension in the patch dome and therefore, if sufficiently long, such a stimulus would allow Piezos to recover from inactivation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about resting tension and inactivation.

claim: A sufficiently long stimulus that zeros membrane tension would allow Piezos to recover from inactivation.
source: From this, we predicted that a small positive pressure stimulus, that precisely compensates the resting curvature, should effectively zero membrane tension in the patch dome and therefore, if sufficiently long, such a stimulus would allow Piezos to recover from inactivation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about resting tension and inactivation.

claim: Robust rapidly-inactivating currents were elicited in cell-attached patches upon release of positive pressure prepulses.
source: Strikingly, with this first prepulse protocol we were able to elicit robust rapidly-inactivating currents in cell-attached patches not during the presence of pressure, but rather upon its release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Current amplitudes upon release of prepulses depended strongly on the prepulse amplitude in a U-shaped manner.
source: The current amplitudes depended strongly on the prepulse amplitude in a U-shaped manner, i.e., currents were maximal after prepulses of ~ +5–6 mmHg and decreased for smaller or larger prepulses (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Currents were maximal after prepulses of ~ +5–6 mmHg.
source: The current amplitudes depended strongly on the prepulse amplitude in a U-shaped manner, i.e., currents were maximal after prepulses of ~ +5–6 mmHg and decreased for smaller or larger prepulses (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: No currents were observed upon release of pressure in cells transfected with empty vector (pcDNA).
source: We never observed currents upon release of pressure in cells transfected with empty vector (pcDNA), indicating that these currents were indeed Piezo1-mediated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The biphasic dependence of current on prepulse pressure amplitude was tightly linked to membrane curvature.
source: Importantly, the biphasic dependence of current on prepulse pressure amplitude was tightly linked to membrane curvature.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Peak currents occurred at or near the minimal curvature for each individual patch.
source: Specifically, we observed for each individual patch that peak currents occurred at or near the minimal curvature, i.e., when the membrane was flattest (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Currents are maximal precisely after prepulses that minimize membrane curvature (R→∞).
source: Averaging data from N = 14 patches further showed that currents are maximal precisely after prepulses that minimize membrane curvature (R→∞) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in current amplitude with prepulse duration followed an exponential time course with τ = 2.4 ± 0.3 s.
source: Using this second prepulse protocol, we found that the increase in current amplitude with prepulse duration followed an exponential time course with τ = 2.4 ± 0.3 s (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The time constant of recovery from inactivation (τ = 2.4 ± 0.3 s) is comparable to the time-dependence of recovery of Piezo2 ion channels from inactivation by whole-cell poking assays.
source: This time constant is comparable to the time-dependence of recovery of Piezo2 ion channels from inactivation by whole-cell poking assays, providing further evidence that the process we are observing reflects recovery from inactivation (Coste et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a citation to Coste et al., 2013.

claim: Under standard recording conditions, a substantial fraction of Piezo ion channels is inactivated prior to pressure stimulation.
source: Importantly, this finding demonstrates that under standard recording conditions, a substantial fraction of Piezo ion channels is inactivated prior to pressure stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the prepulse experiments showing recovery from inactivation.

claim: Human gain-of-function mutations in Piezo1 that reduce channel inactivation also apparently sensitize Piezo1 to pressure stimulation.
source: First, human gain-of-function mutations in Piezo1 that reduce channel inactivation also apparently sensitize Piezo1 to pressure stimulation (Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bae et al., 2013.

claim: Yoda1 both antagonizes inactivation and shifts the P50 curve towards smaller values.
source: Second, the only known chemical Piezo1 agonist, Yoda1, both antagonizes inactivation and shifts the P50 curve towards smaller values (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Syeda et al., 2015.

claim: When preceded by a +5 mmHg prepulse, currents elicited by a subsequent test pulse were greatly increased in amplitude.
source: The effect of the +5 mmHg prepulse on the overall current-pressure relationship was striking: When preceded by a +5 mmHg prepulse, currents elicited by a subsequent test pulse were greatly increased in amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The pressure of half-maximal activation was shifted by ~9 mmHg towards lower pressures with a +5 mmHg prepulse compared to a 0 mmHg prepulse.
source: Additionally, the pressure of half-maximal activation was shifted by ~9 mmHg towards lower pressures (P50 = −16.8 ± 2.8 mmHg with a 0 mmHg prepulse and P50 = −7.7 ± 1.1 mmHg with a +5 mmHg prepulse; N=11; P<0.05) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Prepulses of +10 mmHg did not affect the overall pressure sensitivity as compared to 0 mmHg prepulses.
source: Importantly, prepulses of +10 mmHg did not affect the overall pressure sensitivity as compared to 0 mmHg prepulses (P50 = −16.8 ± 2.8 mmHg with a 0 mmHg prepulse and P50 = −13.5 ± 2.9 mmHg with a +10 mmHg prepulse; N=11; P>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: During the long duration of the prepulse experiment, membrane geometry was sufficiently stable to reversibly and reliably alternate between different membrane curvatures.
source: Importantly, we found that during the long duration of the prepulse experiment, membrane geometry was sufficiently stable to reversibly and reliably alternate between different membrane curvatures (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The tension of half-maximal activation was leftward shifted from T50 = 2.2 ± 0.1 mN/m without a prepulse to T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m with a +5 mmHg prepulse.
source: We found that the tension of half-maximal activation was indeed leftward shifted, from T50 = 2.2 ± 0.1 mN/m without a prepulse (0 mmHg) to T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m with a +5 mmHg prepulse (P<0.001; N=11; Figure 5D,E, and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D, E, and G.

claim: Upon a +10 mmHg prepulse, the T50 was leftward shifted compared to no prepulse, but to a lesser extent than with a +5 mmHg prepulse (T50 = 1.8 ± 0.2 mN/m).
source: Upon a +10 mmHg prepulse, the T50 was also leftward shifted to that without a prepulse, but to a lesser extent than with a +5 mmHg prepulse (T50 = 1.8 ± 0.2 mN/m; P=0.03; Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The slope factor was unaltered by prepulse amplitude.
source: The slope factor was unaltered by prepulse amplitude (0 mmHg prepulse, k = 0.8 ± 0.1; +5 mmHg prepulse, k = 0.7 ± 0.1; P=0.53 vs 0 mmHg; +10 mmHg prepulse, k = 1.1 ± 0.2; P=0.07 vs. 0 mmHg).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The prepulse approach unmasks the inherent tension sensitivity of Piezo1.
source: Altogether, our approach unmasks the inherent tension sensitivity of Piezo1 and demonstrates that it can be substantially modulated by resting membrane tension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the prepulse experiments.

claim: Piezo1 tension sensitivity can be substantially modulated by resting membrane tension.
source: Altogether, our approach unmasks the inherent tension sensitivity of Piezo1 and demonstrates that it can be substantially modulated by resting membrane tension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the prepulse experiments.

claim: In a native and undisturbed cell, resting membrane tension might affect overall sensitivity of Piezo1.
source: Our results imply that in a native and undisturbed cell, the same mechanism might affect overall sensitivity of Piezo1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Similar to the vertebrate mechanosensitive K+ channels TREK-1 and TRAAK, Piezo1 responds robustly to both positive and negative pressure.
source: We found that similar to the vertebrate mechanosensitive K+ channels TREK-1 and TRAAK, Piezo1 responds robustly to both positive and negative pressure (Brohawn et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Brohawn et al., 2014b.

claim: TREK-1 and TRAAK respond robustly to both positive and negative pressure.
source: We found that similar to the vertebrate mechanosensitive K+ channels TREK-1 and TRAAK, Piezo1 responds robustly to both positive and negative pressure (Brohawn et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brohawn et al., 2014b.

claim: Several well-studied mechanosensitive ion channels have been demonstrated to sense lateral membrane tension, including prokaryotic channels MscS and MscL, as well as TREK-1 and TRAAK.
source: Several well-studied mechanosensitive ion channels have previously been demonstrated to sense lateral membrane tension, including prokaryotic channels MscS and MscL, as well as TREK-1 and TRAAK (Brohawn et al., 2014b; Moe and Blount, 2005; Sokabe et al., 1991; Sukharev, 1999; 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezos are distinct from previously identified tension sensors in that they are much larger, with many more predicted transmembrane domains.
source: However, Piezos are distinct from each of these previously identified tension sensors in that they are much larger, with many more predicted transmembrane domains, and in that they share no homology on a primary sequence or overall architectural level (Brohawn et al., 2014a; Coste et al., 2015; Ge et al., 2015; Kamajaya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezos share no homology with previously identified tension sensors on a primary sequence or overall architectural level.
source: However, Piezos are distinct from each of these previously identified tension sensors in that they are much larger, with many more predicted transmembrane domains, and in that they share no homology on a primary sequence or overall architectural level (Brohawn et al., 2014a; Coste et al., 2015; Ge et al., 2015; Kamajaya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Piezo proteins do not contain any amino acid sequences with similarity to any known curvature-sensing proteins.
source: However, Piezo proteins do not contain any amino acid sequences with similarity to any known curvature-sensing proteins, and the recently obtained cryo-electron microscopy structure shows no symmetrical features with respect to the plane of the bilayer, making this possibility unlikely (Antonny, 2011; Ge et al., 2015; McMahon and Boucrot, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The cryo-electron microscopy structure of Piezo1 shows no symmetrical features with respect to the plane of the bilayer.
source: However, Piezo proteins do not contain any amino acid sequences with similarity to any known curvature-sensing proteins, and the recently obtained cryo-electron microscopy structure shows no symmetrical features with respect to the plane of the bilayer, making this possibility unlikely (Antonny, 2011; Ge et al., 2015; McMahon and Boucrot, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Alterations in local curvature induced by asymmetric incorporation of lipids can change the response of tension-gated channels to pressure.
source: Previous reports indicate that alterations in local curvature induced by asymmetric incorporation of lipids can change the response of tension-gated channels to pressure (Perozo et al., 2002); this will also have to be tested for Piezo1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perozo et al., 2002.

claim: Piezo is a unique mechanosensor, as Piezo1 probed in a cellular environment is much more sensitive to tension than MscL and MscS in azolectin liposomes.
source: Our data suggest that Piezo is a unique mechanosensor, as Piezo1 probed in a cellular environment is much more sensitive to tension (T50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 mN/m) than are MscL and MscS in azolectin liposomes (T50 ~5–10 mN/m), although we cannot rule out differences arising from the different local lipid environment in eukaryotic cells versus reconstituted systems (Moe and Blount, 2005; Nomura et al., 2012; Sukharev, 2002; Sukharev et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing experimental data with published values.

claim: Unlike the prokaryotic 'release valves' MscL and MscS, Piezo is able to detect very small changes in membrane tension.
source: Together, our data support the evolutionary need for this novel mechanosensor; unlike the prokaryotic 'release valves' MscL and MscS, Piezo is able to detect very small changes in membrane tension, an ability that is essential for its role in intricate physiological processes ranging from sensing renal and blood flow to detection of light touch (Cahalan et al., 2015; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Ranade et al., 2014b; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: The ability to detect very small changes in membrane tension is essential for Piezo's role in sensing renal and blood flow and detection of light touch.
source: Together, our data support the evolutionary need for this novel mechanosensor; unlike the prokaryotic 'release valves' MscL and MscS, Piezo is able to detect very small changes in membrane tension, an ability that is essential for its role in intricate physiological processes ranging from sensing renal and blood flow to detection of light touch (Cahalan et al., 2015; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Ranade et al., 2014b; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sensitivity of Piezo1 to tension differed in cell-attached versus inside-out patches.
source: Observing Piezo1 activity in multiple patch configurations also allowed us to make several observations. First, sensitivity of Piezo1 to tension differed in cell-attached versus inside-out patches.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing T50 values in different configurations.

claim: The varying amount of cytoskeleton retained in different patch configurations contributes to membrane properties, including tension.
source: One potential explanation for this difference is the varying amount of cytoskeleton retained in the two configurations, which contributes to membrane properties, including tension (Gauthier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gauthier et al., 2012.

claim: Inside-out patches contain less cytoskeleton than cell-attached patches.
source: Consistent with this, we observed lower optical density in inside-out patches, which are known to contain less cytoskeleton (Suchyna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Suchyna et al., 2009.

claim: The cytoskeleton is an important regulator of Piezo1 sensitivity.
source: Together, this predicts that the cytoskeleton is an important regulator of Piezo1 sensitivity, a finding that is reconciled with previous reports that inhibition of actin polymerization with cytochalsin-D inhibits whole-cell Piezo1 currents evoked by direct stimulus with a glass pipette, but increases opening in cell-attached pressure-evoked currents (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of actin polymerization with cytochalasin-D inhibits whole-cell Piezo1 currents evoked by direct stimulus with a glass pipette.
source: Together, this predicts that the cytoskeleton is an important regulator of Piezo1 sensitivity, a finding that is reconciled with previous reports that inhibition of actin polymerization with cytochalsin-D inhibits whole-cell Piezo1 currents evoked by direct stimulus with a glass pipette, but increases opening in cell-attached pressure-evoked currents (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gnanasambandam et al., 2015 and Gottlieb et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of actin polymerization with cytochalasin-D increases opening in cell-attached pressure-evoked Piezo1 currents.
source: Together, this predicts that the cytoskeleton is an important regulator of Piezo1 sensitivity, a finding that is reconciled with previous reports that inhibition of actin polymerization with cytochalsin-D inhibits whole-cell Piezo1 currents evoked by direct stimulus with a glass pipette, but increases opening in cell-attached pressure-evoked currents (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gnanasambandam et al., 2015 and Gottlieb et al., 2012.

claim: Inactivation is irreversibly lost with repeated stimulation of Piezo1.
source: While the mechanism of Piezo1 inactivation is unknown, a previous study reports that inactivation is irreversibly lost with repeated stimulation, which may explain why we observed the least inactivation in outside-out patches, in which the membrane undergoes the most manipulation prior to assaying activity (Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gottlieb et al., 2012.

claim: The P50 for Piezo1 is typically reported to be ~ −30 mmHg for heterologously expressed Piezo1 in HEK293t cells.
source: For example, while the P50 is typically reported to be ~ −30 mmHg for heterologously expressed Piezo1 in HEK293t cells, in neural stem cells, the P50 was ~−13 mmHg, whereas the P50 was ~−40 mmHg in the breast cancer cell line MCF-7 (Coste et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In neural stem cells, the P50 for Piezo1 was ~−13 mmHg.
source: For example, while the P50 is typically reported to be ~ −30 mmHg for heterologously expressed Piezo1 in HEK293t cells, in neural stem cells, the P50 was ~−13 mmHg, whereas the P50 was ~−40 mmHg in the breast cancer cell line MCF-7 (Coste et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the breast cancer cell line MCF-7, the P50 for Piezo1 was ~−40 mmHg.
source: For example, while the P50 is typically reported to be ~ −30 mmHg for heterologously expressed Piezo1 in HEK293t cells, in neural stem cells, the P50 was ~−13 mmHg, whereas the P50 was ~−40 mmHg in the breast cancer cell line MCF-7 (Coste et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Piezo1 sensitivity is modulated by interaction with other cellular components, which may be differentially expressed.
source: One explanation for this is that Piezo1 sensitivity is modulated by interaction with other cellular components, which may be differentially expressed: For example, Piezo1 mechanosensitivity requires the presence of phosphoinositides, which are depleted over time in excised patches (Borbiro et al., 2015); the integral membrane protein STOML3 also greatly increases Piezo1 sensitivity (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borbiro et al., 2015 and Poole et al., 2014.

claim: Piezo1 mechanosensitivity requires the presence of phosphoinositides.
source: One explanation for this is that Piezo1 sensitivity is modulated by interaction with other cellular components, which may be differentially expressed: For example, Piezo1 mechanosensitivity requires the presence of phosphoinositides, which are depleted over time in excised patches (Borbiro et al., 2015); the integral membrane protein STOML3 also greatly increases Piezo1 sensitivity (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borbiro et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphoinositides are depleted over time in excised patches.
source: One explanation for this is that Piezo1 sensitivity is modulated by interaction with other cellular components, which may be differentially expressed: For example, Piezo1 mechanosensitivity requires the presence of phosphoinositides, which are depleted over time in excised patches (Borbiro et al., 2015); the integral membrane protein STOML3 also greatly increases Piezo1 sensitivity (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borbiro et al., 2015.

claim: The integral membrane protein STOML3 greatly increases Piezo1 sensitivity.
source: One explanation for this is that Piezo1 sensitivity is modulated by interaction with other cellular components, which may be differentially expressed: For example, Piezo1 mechanosensitivity requires the presence of phosphoinositides, which are depleted over time in excised patches (Borbiro et al., 2015); the integral membrane protein STOML3 also greatly increases Piezo1 sensitivity (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Poole et al., 2014.

claim: Resting membrane tension is an additional modulator of Piezo sensitivity.
source: Here, we found that an additional modulator of Piezo sensitivity is resting membrane tension.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Cellular membrane tension varies greatly with cell type.
source: Importantly, cellular membrane tension varies greatly with cell type; even within one cell local tension depends on factors including lipid composition, cytoskeletal contacts, the extracellular matrix, and others (Blumenthal et al., 2014; Hoffman, 2014; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within one cell, local tension depends on factors including lipid composition, cytoskeletal contacts, the extracellular matrix, and others.
source: Importantly, cellular membrane tension varies greatly with cell type; even within one cell local tension depends on factors including lipid composition, cytoskeletal contacts, the extracellular matrix, and others (Blumenthal et al., 2014; Hoffman, 2014; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of tension to modulate sensitivity gives Piezo1 a broad tuning curve that primes it to respond to physiologically relevant changes in tension at different locations.
source: As Piezos are thus under differing tension depending on their cellular expression and localization, the ability of tension to modulate sensitivity gives Piezo1 a broad tuning curve that primes it to respond to physiologically relevant changes in tension at that location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The ability of tension to modulate sensitivity makes Piezos robust sensors of membrane tension in a wide variety of cell types.
source: Importantly, this makes Piezos robust sensors of membrane tension in the remarkably wide variety of cell types in which they are expressed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Inactivation is an important physiological modulator of overall Piezo1 sensitivity.
source: Third, our results also identify inactivation as an important physiological modulator of overall Piezo1 sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: A stimulus that results in a local reduction of membrane tension may lead to increased Piezo activity in this region upon release of this stimulus.
source: Interestingly, the currents we observed after Piezo channels recovered from inactivation during a transient period of zero tension (i.e., +5 mmHg prepulses) may have important physiological relevance: a stimulus that results in a local reduction of membrane tension may lead to increased Piezo activity in this region upon release of this stimulus, perhaps providing a mechanism by which cells can sense not only the onset, but also the offset of a stimulus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The interplay between activation and inactivation may make Piezo1 most sensitive to rapidly applied mechanical stimuli.
source: The interplay between activation and inactivation may also make Piezo1 most sensitive to rapidly applied mechanical stimuli, similar to previous reports for MscS, as slowly applied stimuli will lead to gradual accumulation of channels in inactivated states (Akitake et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and supported by a citation to Akitake et al., 2005.

claim: For MscS, slowly applied stimuli lead to gradual accumulation of channels in inactivated states.
source: The interplay between activation and inactivation may also make Piezo1 most sensitive to rapidly applied mechanical stimuli, similar to previous reports for MscS, as slowly applied stimuli will lead to gradual accumulation of channels in inactivated states (Akitake et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Akitake et al., 2005.

claim: The prepulse protocol provides a useful tool for measuring the inherent mechanosensitivity in different cells irrespective of inactivation kinetics.
source: Finally, we anticipate that our simple prepulse protocol will provide a useful tool for measuring the inherent mechanosensitivity in different cells and irrespective of inactivation kinetics by manipulating the curvature of the membrane to minimize tension prior to testing sensitivity.
evidence: This is a prediction about the utility of the method developed in this study.
